new_statements.quote: [p.161-162] DISSYLLABIC WORDS :- As the final syllable of every word in almost all Indo-Aryan languages is pronounced rather weakly. It generally has no accent which means that the initial syllable gets it. But when the second syllable is weighty than the first, under the influence of a long vowel or a long vowel consonant, it attracts the accent to the second syllable, on the weightage of the syllables described above. [...] But when the vowel ( ā ) comes in the second syllable, the accent is definately on it, as ( ā ) is extraordinarily larger than all other vowels. [p.163] THE WORDS OF THREE SYLLABLES :- We find that :- (1) The final short syllable is never accented.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive word accent computed over a four-grade syllable-weight scale (open-short < open-long < closed-short < closed-long, with ā heaviest of all). Disyllables: accent on the initial syllable by default (final syllables are weak); if the second syllable outweighs the first (long vowel or closed), the accent moves to it; equal weight or heavier first -> initial. Trisyllables: a final short syllable is never accented and a final long one usually is not; initial heavy + medial short -> initial accent; initial short + second long/closed -> second-syllable accent; a few closed-closed patterns take third-syllable accent. Four-syllable words follow the same outline. Monosyllables are accented; enclitics are not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 159: three grades detected (principal, secondary, tertiary = no stress); e.g. 'dudhiyO' has chief accent on the initial syllable, the next syllable practically unstressed, the final syllable a secondary accent; the author marks only primary accent thereafter and notes (p. 159-160) that 'some words.. have two accents', treated later.
new_statements.exceptions: Enclitics (always phrase-bound words such as certain postpositions/conjunctions) carry no accent and have emphatic (accented) vs non-emphatic (enclitic) forms (p. 161); disyllabic types U– and –U are 'balanced' and hard to assign 'in some cases' (p. 162); ā in a second syllable always takes the accent (p. 162); for trisyllables with two initial short syllables accent on a final long syllable is 'doubtful' (p. 163); four-syllable words too few to formulate rules for every case (p. 165).
new_statements.domain_note: Word accent explicitly distinguished from phrase accent and sentence accent (p. 159: 'I have therefore concentrated on the first two types'); rules stated over citation-form words classified by syllable count; phrases of four syllables built from two or more words follow the four-syllable word rules, 'no special accent system for them' (p. 165-166). Stress defined after Daniel Jones as force of utterance; accent said to combine length, stress and intonation (p. 158).
new_statements.identity_note: The only descriptive grammar Glottolog attaches to vagh1246 -- Vyas 1966 -- describes 'Vagheri', the speech of the Vagher (Wagher) community of Okhamandal (Dwarka area, Saurashtra, Gujarat, INDIA; ~15,000 people in 45 villages, 'nowhere else in India'), a Gujarati/Halari/Kachchhi-adjacent variety. The author himself (ch. I p. 8) says the Gujarati 'vaghari' bird-catcher caste name 'does not seem to have any cultural affinity with our Vaghers'. Ethnologue/Glottolog's Vaghri [vgr] is the language of the nomadic Vaghri (Bavri) of Sindh, PAKISTAN. The equation Vagheri-of-Okhamandal = vgr is Glottolog's (HH language code note 'Vaghers of Okhamandal near India-Pakistan border = Vaghri [vgr]') and Wikipedia's, and Wikipedia flags the article 'identity is suspect'. No separate glottocode for Okhamandal Vagheri is known to me. Catalog entry should carry this caveat: the stress statement is first-hand for Okhamandal Vagheri, only by Glottolog's assignment for Sindh Vaghri.
